questions.prompt: What does bytes/token measure for a fixed tokenizer?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: A.** Bytes/token is a sequence-length measure: the average number of input UTF-8 bytes represented by one token ID. Full bit-level compression would also count ID width, the vocabulary, and metadata.

options.text: How many input UTF-8 bytes one token ID represents on average in this text
The full compressed-file size including vocabulary, metadata, and ID packing
The mean probability of the selected token IDs under a language model

questions.prompt: Why does byte-level BPE need no OOV token?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: B.** The base alphabet contains all 256 byte values. Merges only add longer units, so any byte string remains representable without an Out-of-Vocabulary token.

questions.prompt: When can decode(encode(s)) fail to preserve the original spelling?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: C.** With full coverage, the recoverable text is N(s). The teaching BBPE preserves valid UTF-8 without normalization; UNK replacement can lose further information.

questions.prompt: Why does BPE encoding follow learned merge ranks rather than current pair frequency?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: A.** After training, the tokenizer must reproduce the same segmentation expected by the model weights. Frequencies in a new string do not rewrite the merge list.

questions.prompt: How does the o200k_harmony vocabulary size reconcile exactly?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: A.** There are 1,091 special-token names but 1,090 unique IDs because <|endofprompt|> and <|reserved_200018|> alias ID 200018. Ten names are protocol-bearing and 1,081 have reserved form.

questions.prompt: What does tiktoken.encode do by default when input literally contains a registered special-token spelling?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: B.** Special spellings are a protocol boundary. allowed_special admits them as controls; encode_ordinary or disallowed_special=() treats the spelling as ordinary text.

options.text: Always emits the control ID when the spelling matches exactly
Raises by default; the application selects special or ordinary-text handling
Always splits the spelling into characters and ignores the special-token table

questions.prompt: Why is a plain token-to-ID table insufficient to reproduce a deployed tokenizer?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: C.** A tokenizer is a deterministic program, not merely a string table. Changing any component can alter IDs and make input incompatible with model weights.

options.text: Token identifiers change randomly whenever the program is restarted
The embedding matrix must be stored inside the same tokenizer.json file
Normalization, pre-tokenization, ranks, decoder, and special-token policy are also required

questions.prompt: o200k_base defines 200,000 IDs and its maximum ID is 200018. What is n_vocab?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: C.** tiktoken n_vocab is the ID range size. There are 19 holes; this field does not establish a closed model’s embedding-table row count.

questions.prompt: Why does a larger vocab_size not guarantee better tokenization for every language?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: A.** Allocated rows can differ from the defined ID count. Even a larger ordinary-token inventory does not guarantee better segmentation: training data and algorithm rules matter.

questions.explanation: **Correct answer: B.** Regular segmentation changes the inductive bias and can help some numerical tasks. Arithmetic ability still depends on data, architecture, and training.

questions.prompt: A model has vocab_size=16,384 and hidden size=512. How many parameters are in one embedding matrix?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: A.** One matrix has V·d = 16,384·512 = 8,388,608 parameters. An untied output head adds another matrix of the same size.

questions.explanation: **Correct answer: B.** Each occurrence of ID 0 contributes E[0]=[1,0]. Summing gives [2,0]. np.add.at accumulates repeated indices correctly; grad[ids] += ... does not.

questions.prompt: Why is a vision projector only a partial analogue of text tokenization?
questions.explanation: **Correct answer: B.** Both systems create a sequence for a Transformer, but a text tokenizer emits discrete IDs while a typical vision encoder/projector emits continuous representations. Discrete audio codecs are a closer literal analogy.
